content: The serum concentration profile of enalaprilat demonstrates a prolonged terminal phase, which appears to represent a small fraction of the administered dose that is bound to angiotensin-converting enzyme (ACE). The amount of enalaprilat bound to ACE does not increase with higher doses, suggesting the presence of a saturable binding site. The effective half-life for the accumulation of enalaprilat after multiple doses of enalapril maleate is approximately 11 hours. In patients with renal insufficiency, the pharmacokinetics of enalapril and enalaprilat are similar to those in patients with normal renal function until the glomerular filtration rate (GFR) decreases to 30 mL/min or less. When the GFR is ≤30 mL/min, peak and trough levels of enalaprilat increase, the time to reach peak concentration is prolonged, and the time to achieve steady-state may be delayed. At this level of renal impairment, the effective half-life of enalaprilat is extended. Enalaprilat is dialyzable at a rate of 62 mL/min. Studies in dogs indicate that enalapril crosses the blood-brain barrier poorly, if at all, and enalaprilat does not enter the brain. In rats, multiple doses of enalapril maleate do not result in tissue accumulation. However, the milk of lactating rats contains radioactivity following the administration of 14C-enalapril maleate. Additionally, radioactivity has been shown to cross the placenta in pregnant hamsters after administration of labeled enalapril. Neither enalapril maleate nor its active diacid metabolite was found to be mutagenic in the Ames microbial mutagen test, whether or not metabolic activation was present. Enalapril also tested negative in other genotoxicity studies, including the rec-assay, reverse mutation assay with E. coli, sister chromatid exchange in cultured mammalian cells, the micronucleus test in mice, and an in vivo cytogenetic study using mouse bone marrow. No adverse effects on reproductive performance were observed in male and female rats treated with enalapril at doses up to 90 mg/kg/day, which is 26 times the maximum recommended human daily dose (MRHDD) when adjusted for body surface area. In clinical trials involving patients treated with digitalis and diuretics, enalapril therapy led to reductions in systemic vascular resistance, blood pressure, pulmonary capillary wedge pressure, and heart size, while increasing cardiac output and exercise tolerance. Heart rate was either unchanged or slightly reduced, and mean ejection fraction was either unchanged or increased. There was a beneficial effect on the severity of heart failure, as measured by the New York Heart Association (NYHA) classification, as well as on symptoms of dyspnea and fatigue. Hemodynamic improvements were observed after the first dose and appeared to be sustained in uncontrolled studies lasting up to four months. Improvements in exercise tolerance, heart size, and heart failure severity and symptoms were also observed in placebo-controlled studies lasting from eight weeks to over one year. Enalapril is indicated for the treatment of symptomatic heart failure, typically in combination with diuretics and digitalis. In placebo-controlled studies that demonstrated improved survival, patients were titrated as tolerated up to a maximum dose of 40 mg per day, administered in two divided doses. The usual dose range is 5 to 20 mg given twice daily. Doses should be titrated upward, as tolerated, over a period of several days or weeks. The maximum daily dose administered in clinical trials was 40 mg in divided doses.
